Coverage of the brief: statistics (slides 4-7), unsupervised mining (8-9, 12), supervised learning and forecasting (10, 13-14), workflow with the labelled feedback loop (3, 11), second iteration with visualization (11-14), inferences checked in space (country-held-out folds) and time (2021-25 holdout, drift).

## Slide 1: From Snapshots to Trajectories

[Parikshith, 0:00-0:16] We are Team Plot Twist. Our question from A1: did mobile leapfrogging close the digital divide? In A3 we test what we saw, with statistics, clustering and prediction, inside a visual analytics workflow with one feedback loop.

## Slide 2: One question, four sub-questions, one feedback loop

[Varshith, 0:16-0:35] The brief asks for statistics, unsupervised mining and supervised learning inside a workflow with a feedback loop. So we split the question into sub-questions, one per method family, plus the workflow itself. The data is A1's OWID panel: 217 countries, 1960 to 2025.

## Slide 3: The workflow, unrolled: two full iterations joined by one labelled feedback loop

[Parikshith, 0:35-1:01] Keim's diamond drawn as a cycle cannot show which pass produced which finding, so we unroll it into two rows. Iteration 1 runs on the raw data and ends with four inferences, K1. The red edge is the one feedback loop: K1 becomes a data transformation. Iteration 2 repeats data, visualization, models and knowledge on the transformed data, with no self-loops.

## Slide 4: V1  Every region follows the same S-curve, up to 12 years late, and late starters do not catch up

[Parikshith, 1:01-1:23] First, statistics. A logistic S-curve fits 201 of 203 countries. The take-off year differs by region, p of 4 times 10 to the minus 17: Africa takes off in 2017, almost 12 years after Europe. And a later take-off does not mean faster growth. The divide is a delay on one curve.

## Slide 5: V1b  The divide narrowed in relative terms only; low starters close the smallest share of their gap

[Parikshith, 1:23-1:44] Is that delay closing? Relative inequality, the Gini, fell from 0.81 to 0.19. But the absolute gap between the median European and African country peaked at 64 points in 2014 and is still 52, and low starters close the smallest share of their remaining gap. There is no catch-up.

## Slide 6: V2  Broadband has a floor and a non-linear effect; mobile stopped separating countries after 2005

[Parikshith, 1:44-2:06] What separates countries? Nearly 30 percent of country-years have under one broadband line per 100, yet internet use there reaches 30 percent: a floor. Mobile's correlation with internet use fell from 0.88 in 2005 to 0.42 in 2024, while broadband stays at 0.80. Mobile saturated, so it stopped telling countries apart.

## Slide 7: V3  Subscriptions count SIMs, not people, and Fiji's 2023-24 values are a recording artefact

[Parikshith, 2:06-2:22] And mobile counts SIMs, not people: the median country has 1.34 SIMs per owner. Fiji jumps from 111 to 574 subscriptions in two years while ownership stays at 82 percent. That is a recording error, not adoption.

## Slide 8: V5  Three archetypes ordered by connectivity, separated by landlines and broadband, only moderately stable

[Sindhoor, 2:22-2:41] Next, unsupervised mining of the 2024 snapshot. k-means gives three archetypes ordered by connectivity, separated by landlines and broadband, not mobile. But bootstrap ARI is only 0.64, and Ward's best-looking silhouette is fake: one of its clusters is just Fiji and Hong Kong.

## Slide 9: V6  Both detectors rank Fiji first; most anomalies are multi-SIM markets

[Sindhoor, 2:41-2:56] Isolation Forest and LOF both rank Fiji as the top anomaly, independently confirming the error. [DEMO, Mine tab: hover Fiji, about 8 seconds.]

## Slide 10: V7  A raw-infrastructure model explains 86% of variance but leans on broadband alone

[Varshith, 2:56-3:17] Then supervised learning: predict internet share from raw infrastructure. Folds hold out whole countries, so the model is always tested on a country it has never seen. Gradient boosting reaches 11.8 points error, R-squared 0.86. Broadband dominates, shuffling mobile costs almost nothing, and errors are large in mid-adoption countries.

## Slide 11: K1 → FEEDBACK LOOP: each inference becomes a change to the data

[Sindhoor, 3:17-3:50] This is the feedback loop. Four inferences leave iteration 1, and each one changes the data. Fiji is an error: two artefact rules remove 10 cells across all countries. Subscriptions are not people: normalise by owners and cap mobile at 100. History matters: add the landline peak and reshape to trajectories. Broadband has a floor and the gaps are not random: log transform, a floor flag, and imputation inside each training fold. On the right, the transformed data.

## Slide 12: V8  Grouped by PATH, countries form three S-curve archetypes that cut across the 2024 snapshot

[Sindhoor, 3:50-4:11] Iteration 2 clusters each country's whole curve with dynamic time warping. Three archetypes: late starters like Tanzania, the S-curve majority, early saturators like South Korea. Two thirds of Africa are late starters. The clusters separate far better, silhouette 0.52 against 0.35, and 37 of 133 countries change group.

## Slide 13: V10  On identical rows and folds, the transformed data lower error by 14%, most in Asia and Africa

[Varshith, 4:11-4:28] Same countries, same folds, same rows: error falls from 11.77 to 10.16 points, minus 14 percent, most in Asia and Africa. Imputation adds 2,134 usable rows and error reaches 8.84. The ablations show the engineered features carry the gain.

## Slide 14: V12  Forecasts made in 2020 run low; conformal re-calibration restores the cone of uncertainty

[Varshith, 4:28-4:58] Finally, forecasting. Trained up to 2020 and tested on 2021 to 2025, 71 percent of forecasts run low and the 80 percent band covers only 50 percent, because the target drifted after 2020 while the inputs did not. Conformal re-calibration widens the band by 4.7 points and coverage returns to 83 percent. [DEMO, Forecast & drift tab: India, raw versus conformal, about 8 seconds.]

## Slide 15: V14  Answer: the divide is a delay on one S-curve, and fixed infrastructure, not mobile, marks the position

[Parikshith, 4:58-5:19] Putting it together. When: every region is on the same S-curve, 6 to 12 years behind Europe. What: today broadband and the landline peak separate countries, mobile does not. Who: the archetypes differ in fixed infrastructure. And the feedback loop improved every check: error, cluster separation and forecast coverage.

## Slide 16: What we know now, and what we cannot claim

[Varshith, 5:19-5:34] So mobile leapfrogging happened, but it did not close the divide. We cannot claim causation, ownership is mostly imputed, and forecasts assume no further drift. Everything is reproducible with one command. Thank you.

### Slide 17 (hidden appendix): System architecture: one shared core, three analysis modules, every number read from artefacts

How it is built: one shared core module holds the data loading, the artefact rules and the engineered features, so the feedback loop is a single definition. Three analysis modules write tables and figures, and the report, the deck and the browser app only read those artefacts. One command reproduces everything.

### Slide 18 (hidden appendix): V3b  Data are missing not at random, so the method changes between iterations

Before modelling, data quality. Broadband exists only from about 2000, phone ownership only in survey years, and 2025 is almost empty. Crucially, the gaps are not random: country-years without an ownership survey are far less online, 50 against 75 percent. Filling them with an average would bias poor countries upwards, so iteration 1 uses complete cases and iteration 2 uses imputation fitted inside each training fold, plus flags that tell the model a value was missing.

### Slide 19 (hidden appendix): V4  Two axes describe 82% of 2024 connectivity; the mobile axis is stretched by two countries

On the 2024 snapshot of 135 complete countries, PCA puts 64 percent of variance on one connectivity axis, where all five indicators load positively. The second axis is mobile alone, and Fiji and Hong Kong stretch it by themselves.

### Slide 20 (hidden appendix): V9  The transformation removes ten artefact cells and adds history no single-year value contains

This is the first view of iteration 2: what the transformation changed. On the left, the removed cells. In the middle, the engineered features against the raw ones: the history features carry information no single-year value has, and SIMs per owner is noise, so we neutralise it. On the right, coverage, which is why we impute. [DEMO, app tab 2: Fiji raw versus cleaned.]

### Slide 21 (hidden appendix): V8b  The three archetypes are the natural cut of the DTW tree and lie on one timing continuum

Is k equal to 3 justified? The dendrogram of DTW distances says yes: late starters split off at the root and early saturators next. The t-SNE map of the same distances lays the countries on one continuum ordered by timing, from Ethiopia to South Korea, with India, Indonesia and Nigeria on the boundary.

### Slide 22 (hidden appendix): V11  Ownership, broadband and the landline peak drive the model; its errors are geographic

On the left, SHAP ranks phone ownership, log broadband and the landline peak on top; ownership is mostly imputed, so it acts as a composite index. The map shows where infrastructure under- or over-explains adoption. Kosovo is a data gap, not a finding. [DEMO, app tab 3: toggle iteration 1 and 2.]

### Slide 23 (hidden appendix): V13  After 2020 the target drifts past the retraining threshold while the inputs do not

This is the drift chart from the lecture on ML workflows: Population Stability Index per year against a 2015 to 2020 baseline, with thresholds 0.1 and 0.2. After 2020 the target crosses 0.2 while every input stays below until 2023. Same infrastructure, more people online. So we predict, before looking, that the forecast will be too low and too confident.

### Slide 24 (hidden appendix): V12b  The model learned the broadband floor and a history effect; only conformal intervals are calibrated

Two checks on the model. Partial dependence: predictions stay flat while broadband is on the floor and rise between 3 and 30 per 100; the landline history adds 12 points. And the calibration curve tests the intervals at five levels, not one: raw intervals are over-confident everywhere, the conformal ones sit on the diagonal.
